newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ogata says Kabila's repatriation demand unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Ogata says Kabila's repatriation demand unrealistic.

text.p: Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, on Monday said demands from Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila that Rwandan refugees be repatriated within six weeks were "unrealistic."

She also called on the U.N. Security Council to pay attention to Burundi refugees who were facing deprivation in government-run camps when they returned and to deal with armed Rwandan Hutu militia who were fleeing toward Angola.

Ogata spoke to reporters after briefing the council on her staff's weekend meetings with Kabila, who has promised to help in repatriating the refugees after his forces for weeks had denied relief aid groups access to them.
"We face huge obstacles," she said. "The refugees are scattered again and we need time to locate and transport them to Kisingani," the main point for repatriation.
She said some but not all the refugees could be repatriated in six weeks. "It is unrealistic but we will start. I believe in getting things started," she said.
Council President Antonio Monteiro of Portugal said members had found the deadline unacceptable. "It has to match the real situation," he said.

Ogata said 80,000 refugees were located last week south of Kisangani but efforts to repatriate the most vulnerable were repeatedly obstructed. Another 170,000 Rwandan refugees are unaccounted for and 45,000 are from Burundi, she said.
"Once again the refugees were forced to flee following attacks on the camps allegedly by the local population responding to an inflammatory information campaign by (rebel) alliance forces," she said.

The rebels under Kabila have captured half of Zaire with little resistance from government troops. They are allied with Rwanda's Tutsi-led government, while most of the refugees are Hutus who fled after massacres in Zaire in mid-1990 in which Hutu militants killed more than half a million Tutsis.
Among them were some of the militia who instigated the massacres, but many of the refugees are considered innocent of the massacres.

Ogata said some former Hutu army members were moving deeper into Zaire and had reached the Angolan border, where they were reported to be threatening local Zairians. She said her office excluded them from refugee protection, but the international community "should carefully examine what can be done with this group."

She criticised Burundi's Tutsi military government, which engineered a coup last summer, saying returning refugees were being relocated or regrouped and could not feed themselves. For aid agencies to do so, she said, meant compromising "with the military strategy of the government."
"At the very least the government should be required to set measurable benchmarks for the treatment of this population and for the progressive closure of (their) camps," she said.
Ogata told the council she was disturbed at reports of abuses against refugees, particularly children reported on Monday to have been abducted by armed men from a pediatric hospital near Bukavu.

"I am distubed about the apparently organised and systematic attacks on refugees who approach our reception and transit centres requesting to be repatriated and about reports that locals are prevented form helping refugees and being forced instead to chase them away," she said.
Looking back, Ogata said humanitarian agencies should not have been left alone to deal with the crisis in Zaire.

"Humanitarian activities depend upon political and sometimes military action. That is why I have called for the establishment of a rapid deployment capability," she said. "Humanitarian actors should not be left alone to take unresolved political questions and dangerous security situations."
